My story

The choices along the way.

01 / HackerEarth · Sales

A first job in software sales

In my final year studying computer science, HackerEarth hired me to do market research. That turned into a sales role. I spent my time figuring out which companies in the US and Canada might need our software, who to talk to, and how to get a conversation going. One of those conversations led to a $150K deal. In all, I helped bring in more than $315K in signed business.

By the time I left, I wanted to build a company of my own. I also wanted to try my hand at the thing I’d spent four years studying.

02 / Capgemini · Engineering

Putting my degree to work

That’s why I joined Capgemini. I worked on the SAP Environment, Health and Safety system for Bayer Germany, a Fortune 500 client. I investigated and fixed issues that business users ran into, and on the development side I worked with ABAP and SQL. I’d seen what it took to sell software. Now I was learning what it took to keep it working for the people who relied on it.

03 / CloudEagle · Sales

A day job and a night shift

I decided to go abroad for my MBA because I wanted to understand more of how a business runs. First, I had to pay for the move. Capgemini was my day job, and at night I worked in sales for CloudEagle. Their customers were in North America, so my evenings lined up with their workday. The sales incentives helped cover my moving expenses, and I moved to Vancouver.

04 / Accounting Bridge · Operations

Whatever needed doing

While studying part-time for my MBA, I worked at Accounting Bridge. My title was Office Administrator, but I was usually the person who picked up whatever needed doing. I spoke with clients in Canada and followed up with accountants and bookkeepers across Canada and India to get them answers. I helped with bookkeeping, digitized records, and built Zapier automations for marketing.

When we were making the firm’s podcast, I helped shoot the episodes, coordinated with the editor, and uploaded the finished episodes across platforms.

05 / Bidfast · Product engineering

Why I put my own startup on hold

By then, I was spending a lot of my own time building with AI. I’d started Cogtics with the intention of making it my startup. The question behind it was simple. If you put the signed contract, the sales record, and the invoice next to each other, did the customer actually get billed for what they agreed to buy?

Then I came across the problem behind Bidfast. Before a contractor can price a job, someone has to go through the drawings and work out what materials the job calls for and in what quantities. I wanted to see how much of that work we could take off their hands. It was a bigger and more technically interesting problem to me, enough that I put Cogtics aside and joined Bidfast as its first technical employee. My hands-on work with AI was part of what got me hired.

I was there from the beginning. I sat with contractors to understand how they put bids together, then built a product they could try on their drawings. One of the hardest parts was teaching the software to recognize electrical symbols using the lines and shapes already embedded in a PDF. I built that engine, the screen where an estimator could check its counts, and the services that ran it on AWS. I gave demos and worked directly with our first client and the founder to decide what needed to change.

What’s next

I like being in the room
with the customer.

At HackerEarth, I had to earn the conversation. At Capgemini, I had to fix the issue someone was calling about. At Bidfast, I could sit down with a contractor, understand what was slowing them down, and build something they could test. That’s the part I’d like to keep doing.
